title: Prevalence of Common Diabetes Mellitus Misinformation Exposure, Cognitive Attitude, and Intention to Share Information Among Patients in a Primary Care Unit
screen_reason: Cross-sectional questionnaire of 107 Thai type 2 diabetes outpatients asked whether they had encountered each of 13 expert-validated false diabetes statements. Self-reported encounter shares are RECALL exposure with a population denominator; the paper reports them only as a range across the 13 items (19.6% to 94.4%), the per-item values living in an unreadable figure. Belief and sharing-intention results are excluded by the protocol.

estimates.platform: paper questionnaire administered in a primary care unit (no platform)
estimates.date: questionnaires completed December 2023 to February 2024 (two-phase study ran April 2023 to May 2024)
estimates.measure_type: % of type 2 diabetes outpatients who reported having encountered each of 13 false diabetes statements, reported as the range across items
estimates.value_raw: Exposure to misinformation ranged from 19.6% to 94.4% across the 13 questionnaire items
estimates.denominator: 107 patients with type 2 diabetes attending the primary care unit at Songklanagarind Hospital, southern Thailand
estimates.definition: participant reported having encountered the stated false claim, from any of five listed sources (television/radio, online media, patients with diabetes, people without diabetes, healthcare providers); one exposure item per misinformation statement
estimates.misinfo_def: In this study, the term "misinformation" refers specifically to inaccurate or false content that is shared with or communicated to patients, while "misconceptions" denote the resulting incorrect beliefs held by patients
estimates.source_quote: The prevalence of exposure to misinformation among patients with T2DM was highly variable, ranging from 19.6% to 94.4% (Figure 1).
estimates.page_loc: Section 3.2 Prevalence of Exposure and Intention to Share Misinformation on T2DM (p. 4); Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: The 13 false statements were not judged by respondents: they were generated by thematic analysis of 14 qualitative interviews with physicians, nurses, dietitians and patients, then validated for content by three independent experts in diabetes care and health communication (all Item-Objective Congruence values > 0.5), piloted on 32 patients, Cronbach's alpha 0.79. Respondents only reported whether they had encountered each statement, so the veracity ground truth is expert, while the exposure measure itself is self-report.
estimates.moderator_quote: Participants were recruited through invitation posters at the hospital. After the informed consent process, they completed a paper-based questionnaire, with data collection being anonymous. ... Content validity was established through an Item-Objective Congruence (IOC) index assessed by three independent experts in diabetes care and health communication.
estimates.notes: range_not_point because the paper gives only the minimum and maximum across the 13 items; the per-item percentages exist only in Figure 1, which is an image and not recoverable from the text. No overall 'exposed to at least one item' figure and no mean exposure score is reported anywhere. The very wide range is item-driven, not sampling-driven: symptom-perception items were near-universal and medication-side-effect items much rarer. population_scope = other because the denominator is a clinical outpatient sample (mean age 64.5, 45.8% primary education only, 58.9% earning under THB 10,000/month), not a general population; an adjudicator preferring general_public should note that caveat rather than lose it. ground_truth changed from researcher_coding to self_report to satisfy the protocol rule that a RECALL row is always self_report: what the respondent contributes, and what the percentage is a share of, is a self-reported encounter. The expert provenance of the 13 false statements themselves is kept in ground_truth_detail, because it is unusually strong here (interview-derived items, three independent expert validators, IOC > 0.5, pilot, alpha 0.79) and is the reason the original coding said researcher_coding.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Group-level exposure distributions are reported but are score distributions, not 'any exposure' shares: 31.8% of participants had an exposure score of 3 out of 4 items in G1 (medication side effects) and 82.2% scored the full 2 points in G4 (symptom perception, meaning exposed to both items). The G4 figure is close to an 'exposed to all items in this domain' prevalence and an adjudicator may want it as a second row; I left it out because it is a specific score point in a distribution rather than the headline prevalence, and because taking one score point from a multi-category distribution risks the sub-row problem R2 warns about. (2) Sharing figures (77.6% likely to share the asymptomatic-control claim, 76.6% the sugary-drink claim, 4.7% the insulin-exercise claim, 46.7% with a sharing score of 0 in G2, 65.4% intending to share both G4 items) are all HYPOTHETICAL intentions measured at the moment of reading, explicitly independent of prior exposure, and are excluded by the protocol. (3) Belief figures (89.7% agreed with Q13, 87.8% with Q12, 59.8% disagreement with Q8) are belief in false claims, also excluded. (4) Table 3 source shares (people without diabetes 46.21%, patients with diabetes 22.28%, healthcare providers 12.69%, online media 11.69%, TV/radio 7.12%) are percentages of the 1,095 recorded exposure instances, not of the 6,955 possible instances the table footnote names; they describe where misinformation came from, not how much there was. The abstract's word-of-mouth figure of 81.18% is a cross-category sum of the three person sources, which R8 forbids. (5) An overall exposure density of 1,095/6,955 = 15.7% is computable but rests on a cross-category sum I am not allowed to make.

rob.design: Two-phase mixed-methods study in one primary care unit (Songklanagarind Hospital, southern Thailand), April 2023 to May 2024. Phase I: 14 qualitative interviews (2 physicians, 2 nurses, 2 dietitians, 8 patients) to saturation, generating 13 misinformation items in four domains. Phase II: paper questionnaire completed by 107 T2DM patients recruited by hospital posters between December 2023 and February 2024, so a convenience clinic sample with no sampling frame and no response rate reported. Instrument validated by three experts (all IOC > 0.5), piloted on 32 patients, Cronbach's alpha 0.79. Exposure is self-reported recall with no time window specified and no recall-period anchor, which limits comparability. Single site, single disease, older and lower-income sample.
rob.item6_quote: In this study, the term "misinformation" refers specifically to inaccurate or false content that is shared with or communicated to patients, while "misconceptions" denote the resulting incorrect beliefs held by patients, and "lack of knowledge" refers to gaps where patients have not received any information.
rob.item10_quote: The prevalence of exposure to misinformation among patients with T2DM was highly variable, ranging from 19.6% to 94.4% (Figure 1).
